books.section: Topic 6.7 Labor in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4954-4964 (work stoppages, workers involved)

rationales.A: From 1884 to 1886, stoppages rose from 485 to 1,572 and workers from 165,000 to 610,000, a break with earlier years.
rationales.B: Stoppages hit their highest level in 1886, not their lowest.
rationales.C: Workers involved range from 130,000 to 610,000, so they did not stay the same.
rationales.D: The table shows hundreds of stoppages in every year from 1881 on.
rationales.general:
A turning point needs a break, not a steady line.
1. From 1881 to 1884, stoppages stay near 500 and workers near 150,000.
2. In 1886, stoppages reach 1,572, more than triple the 1884 figure.
3. Workers involved reach 610,000, nearly four times the 1884 figure.
4. That sudden jump is the break a turning-point claim needs.
Remember: a turning point is a sharp change, so compare the year with the years before it.

stem: A historian argues that 1886 was a turning point for the labor movement. Which evidence from the table best supports that claim?
